projects.title: Alarm Clock with RTC
projects.blurb: A real-time clock chip keeps the time on a 4-digit 7-segment display. Set the alarm with the Hours and Minutes buttons, arm it with Alarm, and the buzzer sounds at the hour.

/**

   Clock Configuration File.
*/

#ifndef __CONFIG_H__
#define __CONFIG_H__

/**
   Change to 0 for running without an external RTC (Real time clock)
*/
#define USE_RTC 1

/**
   Your 7-Segment display type: COMMON_ANODE or COMMON_CATHODE
*/
#define DISPLAY_TYPE COMMON_ANODE

/**
   For how long should we show the alarm status (on/off)?
*/
const int ALARM_STATUS_DISPLAY_TIME = 1000; /* ms */

/**
   For how long should we show the alarm hour?
*/
const int ALARM_HOUR_DISPLAY_TIME = 2500; /* ms */

/**
   For how long should we display the snooze screen?
*/
const int SNOOZE_DISPLAY_TIME = 500; /* ms */

/**
   How many minutes to snooze the alarm for?
*/
const int SNOOZE_TIME = 9; /* minutes */

/**
   The default Alarm hour (for non-RTC mode)
*/
const int DEFAULT_ALARM_HOUR = 9;

#endif /* __CONFIG_H__ */

working: The 7-segment display shows HHMM from the RTC, with the colon blinking once a second.
Hour and Minute retune the shown time; Alarm arms or disarms, then shows " on"/" off" and the alarm time.
At the alarm hour the siren sounds: a short Alarm press snoozes 9 minutes (four circles), a long hold stops it.

projects.title: Electronic Safe
projects.blurb: Three buttons are the combination dial: enter A, C, B in order to unlock. A wrong digit buzzes and the attempt resets.
working: The red LED is lit while locked; nothing else happens until three digits land.
A, then C, then B turns the green LED on for two seconds and prints "unlocked".
Any wrong digit buzzes three times and the attempt starts over.

projects.title: Servo Dashboard
projects.blurb: A slide potentiometer becomes a steering wheel: the servo horn follows the knob and three LEDs show which third of the travel it is in.
working: The horn tracks the knob from end stop to end stop, never asked past 10–170.
Exactly one of the three LEDs is lit, marking the third of the travel.
The serial monitor reports both numbers: the knob reading and the horn angle.

projects.title: Parking Sensor
projects.blurb: An ultrasonic ranger watches the bench: LEDs mark far, near, and too close, and the buzzer complains inside 30 cm. Turn the distance knob to drive closer.
working: The serial monitor reports centimetres that follow the distance knob.
Green means something is out there, yellow inside a metre, red inside 30 cm.
Inside 30 cm the buzzer beeps twice a second; a timed-out echo reads 0 and lights nothing.

projects.title: Weather Station
projects.blurb: A temperature-humidity sensor reports to a character LCD and the serial log. Turn the knobs on the part — or warm it with a fingertip on the bench — and watch both numbers move.
working: The LCD shows temperature on line one and humidity on line two.
Turning the part knobs moves both numbers within a couple of seconds.
The serial monitor logs one line per reading: the DHT’s temperature and humidity, and the one-wire sensor’s own.

projects.title: Shift Register
projects.blurb: A 74HC595 turns two pins into eight. The byte goes in over the SPI bus, the latch line copies it to the outputs, and a row of LEDs chases along behind it.
working: The eight LEDs chase from Q0 to Q7, one every 150 milliseconds.
The chip's register moves the bits toward Q7, so the byte that lights the first LED is the one with its lowest bit set.
The serial log says when the chase starts.

projects.title: RFID Reader
projects.blurb: An MFRC522 card reader on the SPI bus. The sketch turns the antenna on, asks for a card, and reads the answer out of the chip’s FIFO — or the timeout when its field is empty.
working: The serial log opens with the chip’s version, 92, read back over the bus.
With an empty field every request times out and the log says so, once a second.
Put a card in the field and the answer arrives in the FIFO: 4 and 0, the ATQA of a MIFARE Classic.

projects.title: Four-Digit Display
projects.blurb: A TM1637 module and four digits. The chip scans the display itself, so a sketch writes the segment patterns into its registers and the glass shows them: two wires instead of twelve.
working: The glass counts the seconds, one a second, on four digits.
The colon is the decimal point of the second digit, which is the only colon this module has.
The serial log says the same number the glass shows.

projects.title: Stepper Motor
projects.blurb: An A4988 driver and a stepper motor. The chip has a translator behind it: a pulse on STEP moves the motor one step and DIR says which way, so the sketch never writes a phase table.
working: The shaft turns one step for every pulse the sketch sends.
Twenty steps one way and twenty the other, so the shaft turns back and forth.
The serial log counts the steps the sketch sent.

projects.title: Microstepping
projects.blurb: The same A4988 and motor, with the microstep-select pins high. Sixteen pulses make one full step, and the coil currents follow the chip’s sine table instead of a binary phase.
working: Sixteen pulses turn the shaft one full step, 7.5 degrees.
Each pulse is 0.46875 degrees, a sixteenth of a step.
The coil drive follows a sine table, so a winding spends part of the cycle between the rails instead of only at the supply.

projects.title: I/O Expander
projects.blurb: A PCF8574 and eight LEDs. The board has run out of pins, so the expander makes eight more out of the two on the I²C bus: the sketch writes one byte and the ports follow it.
working: The eight lights show the counter in binary, one bit each.
One byte goes out over the bus for every change.
The serial log says the number the lights are showing.

projects.title: Sixteen-Light Counter
projects.blurb: An MCP23017 makes sixteen pins out of the two on the I²C bus. Each port has a direction register, so the sketch clears the direction bits first; only then does the latch drive the LEDs.
working: The sixteen lights show the counter in binary, eight on each port.
The direction registers are cleared first; a latch written while a pin is an input moves nothing.
The serial log prints the number the two ports are showing.

projects.title: One Pin, Sixteen Inputs
projects.blurb: A button sits on an MCP23017 port, and the expander watches it itself. When the button moves the chip pulls INTA, so the sketch reads one pin it already has instead of asking the expander over I²C on every pass of loop().
working: The serial log says the expander is watching PA0, and nothing else until the button is touched.
A press pulls INTA low, the sketch reads the port, and the light comes on with a press line in the log.
Releasing the button raises the port again, and the same path puts the light out.

projects.title: Sixteen-Level Dimmer
projects.blurb: A PCA9685 turns one I²C pair into sixteen PWM channels. Each channel compares the chip’s free-running counter against its own ON and OFF counts, so the sketch sets a duty rather than a pin level; the lights step from one sixteenth to full.
working: The sixteen lights step from one sixteenth of the frame to full on.
The serial log lists the sixteen duties, one sixteenth through full.
The light that is fully on never switches; the rest run at 50 frames a second.

projects.title: Precision Clock
projects.blurb: A DS3231 keeps the time and reports whether it lost power. The sketch reads the oscillator flag first, sets the clock if it has to, then reads the die temperature the chip measures for itself.
working: The serial log reports the lost-power flag, sets the clock, then prints the time it now keeps.
The light toggles with the seconds register, so the clock is driving the board.
Turn the Die temperature knob and the next reading changes: the chip measures itself in quarter-degree steps.

projects.title: Thermocouple
projects.blurb: A MAX6675 amplifier and a thermocouple. The chip reads the probe and hands the reading out over the bus: the sketch shifts out a dummy byte and takes sixteen bits back, four of them status and twelve the temperature in quarter-degree steps.
working: The log carries the probe\u2019s temperature, a quarter of a degree at a time.
Turn the probe knob and the reading follows it.
The sketch reads sixteen bits and throws four of them away.

projects.title: DAC Converter
projects.blurb: An MCP4725 and the board’s own analog input. The bench can measure a voltage; this is the part that makes one — the sketch writes twelve bits over the bus and the chip holds the level, and the board reads it back on an analog pin.
working: The output walks from the ground to the supply in sixteen steps.
The board reads the voltage back on an analog pin, and the log says what it read.
The reading is the code, in the board’s own ten bits.

projects.title: EEPROM
projects.blurb: A 24LC256 and a counter that lives in it. The chip is not a register file: the sketch writes an address and then the bytes at it, which is the shape almost every memory has.
working: The count climbs, and it climbs by one every time.
The counter lives in the memory, not in the sketch: a chip that forgot would start the count again.
The address is sixteen bits, so it takes two bytes on the bus.

projects.title: LED Matrix
projects.blurb: An 8x8 matrix with a MAX7219 behind it. Each of the eight columns is a register, each bit of it is a row, and the whole picture is eight register writes.
working: A heart beats on the matrix: two frames, a wide one and a narrow one.
Each frame is eight writes of an address and a byte, latched by chip-select when the SPI transaction ends.
The serial monitor says when the beat starts.

projects.title: Nokia 5110
projects.blurb: The phone display, sold as a breakout: 84 by 48 pixels of glass behind a PCD8544, driven over four wires. The chip keeps the picture in its own memory, so the whole wave is a run of address-and-byte writes.
working: The glass shows a sine wave: one lit pixel per column, on the row the wave is at, and the wave walks sideways.
The picture is 84 columns of chip memory in six banks of eight rows, and every frame clears all six banks before the wave is written again.
The backlight pin is left unconnected on purpose: it is an LED on the module, and the PCD8544 drives the glass itself, so the wave shows without it.
On this bench the data/command state travels with the byte, so a command goes out as SPI.transfer(value, 0) and a byte of display memory as SPI.transfer(value, 1).

projects.title: Reaction Timer
projects.blurb: Press to arm, wait for the light, then press as fast as you can: the serial monitor reports your latency in milliseconds. Jump the gun and it calls the false start.
working: Press once to arm; the light comes on two to five seconds later.
The serial monitor reports your latency in milliseconds on a clean run.
Pressing early prints "false start" and the round restarts.

projects.title: Network Clock
projects.blurb: The board has no clock of its own, so it asks the network for the time and puts the answer on the screen. Join, ask, wait, read: the waiting is the part that makes it a network program.
working: The serial monitor reports the address the bench network handed out.
The panel shows that address, then the time it fetched, once a second.
Stop the network and the loop reports "network failed" rather than freezing.

projects.title: Sensor Feed
projects.blurb: A sensor on the network publishes a temperature. The board subscribes, reads it without ever blocking, and tells the sensor how often it wants the next one — both directions of a network program.
working: The serial monitor reports the subscription and the order it placed with the sensor.
Then it logs a temperature every two seconds — the cadence the board asked for.
The panel shows the latest reading as it arrives, and the bench stays responsive: the loop never waits.

projects.title: Network Weather
projects.blurb: One board asks two services for their data: the network clock for the time, and a network sensor for temperature and humidity. A single radio means one request at a time, so the loop rotates between hosts and keeps drawing while the next answer is in flight.
working: The serial monitor reports the join, then cycles through "time", "temp" and "humidity" as each answer arrives.
The panel shows one value from each host: the clock at ntp.noesis, and the sensor at sensor.noesis.
Only one request is in flight at a time, and the last value stays on the panel while the next one is pending.

projects.title: Live Weather
projects.blurb: The same poll loop, pointed at a real host: open-meteo, keyless and CORS-clean, reached because this build opted into the live network. The request leaves your machine — a GET, no credentials — and it fails like any other host when the network or the server is not there.
working: The panel names the endpoint before the first request: this one leaves the machine.
The serial prints the JSON open-meteo answered, and the panel draws it — a temperature nobody could know without asking.
Pull the network cable, and the loop reports "no answer" instead of freezing: a real host fails like a bench host.

projects.title: Soil Moisture Probe
projects.blurb: A sensor the bench has no model for, written as a script and carried in the circuit file itself: turn the Moisture knob and the Uno reads it on A0 — the script is the sensor.
working: The serial prints a moisture percentage twice a second, and the inspector shows the probe with its knob.
Turn Moisture down and the reading follows: the script reads the knob, the netlist holds the divider, and the ADC reads it back.
It is a part from the circuit file, not the catalogue — the bench never had a soil probe built in.

projects.title: Instrument Bench
projects.blurb: Three instruments on one pair of wires: a barometer for the weather, a current monitor for the supply, and a sixteen-bit converter for whatever analogue signal you have. The barometer speaks the register protocol, so the compensation the datasheet prints is in the sketch.
working: The serial log prints one line a reading: the pressure and temperature off the barometer, the current and the power off the monitor, and the converter counts.
Turn the Pressure and Temperature knobs on the barometer and both numbers move: the chip reports raw counts and the sketch does the arithmetic.
Turn the Current knob on the monitor and the current and the power move together, because the power is the current times the bus voltage.

projects.title: Environment Bench
projects.blurb: Three weather sensors on one pair of wires: a light meter, a thermometer, and a temperature/humidity sensor whose readings carry their own CRC. Each one speaks its datasheet protocol directly, from a one-byte command to a six-byte frame.
working: The serial log prints one line a reading: the light in lux, the thermometer in degrees, and the humidity sensor with its CRC verdict.
Turn the Light knob and the lux follows: the chip is in continuous mode, so every read is the current light.
Turn the Temperature and Humidity knobs on the SHT31 and the next measurement follows; the TMP102 has its own Temperature knob, read on every pass.
The CRC is recomputed in the sketch from the two data bytes, and the line ends in "crc ok" only when both words agree.

projects.title: Barometer
projects.blurb: A BMP280 barometer on the I2C bus. The sketch reads the chip id, starts a pressure and temperature measurement, reads the raw counts, and applies the datasheet's compensation with calibration coefficients read from the chip itself. Pressure and temperature print to the serial log, and a light comes on above one thousand hectopascals.
working: The serial log reports the chip id (0x58) and then pressure in hPa and temperature in degrees.
Turn the Pressure knob and the reading follows, within a hectopascal.
Turn the Temperature knob and the reading follows, within a tenth of a degree.
Above one thousand hectopascals the light comes on; below it, the light goes out.

projects.title: Thermometer
projects.blurb: An LM35 analog temperature sensor on A0. The sketch reads the voltage, converts it to degrees, and prints it to the serial log. A light comes on above thirty degrees, so the operator can see the reading without opening the monitor.
working: The serial log reports the temperature in whole degrees, following the part's Temperature knob.
Turn the knob past thirty and the light comes on; turn it back down and the light goes out.
The count in the log matches the voltage on A0: ten millivolts per degree.

projects.title: Distance Sensor
projects.blurb: A VL53L0X time-of-flight distance sensor on I2C. The sketch starts a ranging measurement, reads the distance in millimetres, and prints it. A light comes on within one metre.
working: The serial log reports the chip id (0xEE) and then the distance in millimetres.
Turn the Distance knob and the reading follows, within a millimetre.
Within one metre the light comes on; beyond it, the light goes out.

projects.title: Environment Station
projects.blurb: A BME280 environment sensor on I2C � temperature, pressure and humidity from one breakout. The sketch reads calibration coefficients, applies the datasheet compensation, and prints all three readings. A light comes on above 25�C.
working: The serial log reports the chip id (0x60) and then temperature, pressure and humidity.
Turn the Temperature knob and the reading follows, within a hundredth of a degree.
Turn the Pressure knob and the pressure reading follows; turn the Humidity knob and the humidity reading follows.
Above 25�C the light comes on; below it, the light goes out.

projects.title: Soil Moisture Monitor
projects.blurb: A soil moisture sensor on A0. The sketch reads the analog count, converts it to percent, and prints it to the serial log. A light comes on when the soil is dry enough to need watering.
working: The serial log reports the moisture in percent, following the part's Moisture knob.
Turn the knob below forty percent and the light comes on; turn it back up and the light goes out.
The percent in the log matches the ADC count on A0.

projects.title: Weather Sensor
projects.blurb: An AHT20 environment sensor on I2C � temperature and humidity from one breakout. The sketch starts a measurement and reads the raw counts. A light comes on in wet air.
working: The serial log reports the humidity and temperature raw counts.
Turn the Temperature knob and the reading follows.
Turn the Humidity knob and the reading follows.
In wet air above fifty percent the light comes on; below it, the light goes out.

projects.title: Air Quality Monitor
projects.blurb: An SCD40 CO2 sensor on I2C � carbon dioxide, temperature and humidity from one breakout. The sketch starts periodic measurement and reads three words with their CRCs. A light comes on when the CO2 climbs above 1250 ppm.
working: The serial log reports the CO2, temperature and humidity raw counts.
Turn the CO2 knob and the reading follows.
Turn the Temperature and Humidity knobs and the readings follow.
Above 1250 ppm the light comes on; below it, the light goes out.

projects.title: Pulse Monitor
projects.blurb: A MAX30102 pulse oximeter on I2C � heart rate and blood oxygen from one fingertip module. The sketch starts the PPG and reads infrared and red counts. A light comes on with a strong pulse.
working: The serial log reports the chip id (0x15) and then infrared and red counts.
Turn the Heart rate knob and the counts follow.
Turn the SpO2 knob and the counts follow.
With a strong pulse the light comes on; with a weak one, it goes out.

projects.title: Gas Sensor
projects.blurb: A BME680 gas sensor on I2C � temperature, pressure, humidity and gas resistance from one breakout. The sketch starts a measurement and reads the raw counts. A light comes on when the gas resistance drops.
working: The serial log reports the chip id (0x61) and then pressure, temperature, humidity and gas counts.
Turn the Gas resistance knob and the reading follows.
Turn the Temperature, Pressure and Humidity knobs and the readings follow.
When the gas resistance drops low enough, the light comes on.

projects.title: Gesture Sensor
projects.blurb: An APDS9960 gesture sensor on I2C � gesture, proximity and ambient light from one breakout. The sketch reads the data registers. A light comes on when a hand is close.
working: The serial log reports the chip id (0xAB) and then proximity, ambient and gesture.
Turn the Proximity knob and the reading follows.
Turn the Ambient knob and the reading follows.
When a hand is close the light comes on; far away, it goes out.

projects.title: Compass
projects.blurb: A BNO055 absolute orientation sensor on I2C � heading, pitch and roll with a magnetometer and sensor fusion. The sketch puts it in NDOF mode and reads the orientation. A light comes on when the heading turns past a quarter turn.
working: The serial log reports the chip id (0xA0) and then heading, pitch and roll.
Turn the Heading knob and the reading follows.
Turn the Pitch and Roll knobs and the readings follow.
Past ninety degrees the light comes on; below it, the light goes out.

projects.title: Tilt Sensor
projects.blurb: An ADXL335 analog accelerometer on A0, A1 and A2. The sketch reads the three axes, converts the counts back to g, and prints them. A light comes on when the X tilt is strong.
working: The serial log reports X, Y and Z in g, following the part's knobs.
Turn the X knob past one g and the light comes on.
At rest the axes read near zero, mid-rail, as the chip does.

projects.title: Gas Detector
projects.blurb: An MQ-2 gas sensor on A0. The sketch reads the analog count, converts it back to ppm, and prints it. A light comes on when the concentration rises above 400 ppm.
working: The serial log reports gas concentration in ppm, following the part's Gas concentration knob.
Turn the knob past 400 ppm and the light comes on.
The ppm in the log matches the ADC count on A0.
